title: Casper and the Songbook
premise: Elodie Thackeray, a lighthouse keeper's granddaughter who writes romance novels under a male pseudonym, is assigned an anonymous pen-pal exchange through her small-town literary society—only to discover her correspondent is Casper Vane, the developer whose family firm plans to buy and demolish the lighthouse she calls home. Their letters, written without names, become the one place each can be honest: he confesses his complicity in his family's corruption, she confesses that her celebrated novels are borrowed from a life she's too afraid to live. When identities are revealed at the autumn festival, betrayal and attraction collide, forcing Casper to choose between inheritance and integrity. He publicly kills the development, loses his family, and stays past the last train of the festival season to tell Elodie that love, for once, should be in the present tense.
about_author: Quentin Eastwick is the pen name of a former coastal archivist who spent a decade cataloguing shipwreck letters before turning to fiction. Eastwick writes romances about people who mistake silence for safety, and lives within sight of a working light.

chapters.title: The Last Train Schedule
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She tends the decommissioned lighthouse, dodges her grandmother's questions about why her novels stopped, and grudgingly signs up for the Saltmere Literary Society's anonymous winter pen-pal exchange. Emotional beat: comfortable isolation revealed as a habit, not a choice.

chapters.title: Correspondent Unknown
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Newly arrived to oversee Vane Development's Harbour Quarter acquisition, he joins the exchange on a publicist's advice to soften his image. His first letter is corporate polish; Elodie's reply skewers it mercilessly. Beat: two guarded people amused despite themselves.

chapters.title: Rules of Tense
chapters.summary: Alternating letters. They negotiate terms: no names, no professions, no present-tense confessions. Elodie writes as 'E,' Casper as 'C.' Each lies by omission about exactly one thing. Beat: intimacy built on architecture of avoidance.

chapters.title: What the Light Remembers
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Her grandmother reveals the lighthouse's deed is tangled in old debt, and surveyors appear on the point. Elodie recognizes the Vane crest on their clipboards. Beat: dread arriving in daylight.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. At a town meeting, he watches Elodie argue against the development with fierce eloquence—and finds himself admiring the enemy his firm sent him to defeat. Beat: first crack in loyalty.

chapters.title: Letters Against the Tide
chapters.summary: Their correspondence deepens; 'C' admits he's complicit in something he can't name, 'E' admits her published love stories are inventions covering an old heartbreak. Neither sees the other's face in the words. Beat: mutual confession without recognition.

chapters.title: Inheritance of Ruin
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Flashback chapter: his father forging environmental assessments, Casper signing off at twenty-three because refusal meant exile. Now his father demands the lighthouse parcel by quarter's end. Beat: power inherited as a debt.

chapters.title: The Novelist's Mask
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A young reader recognizes her prose style at the bookshop and nearly outs her pseudonym. Elodie realizes her anonymity, like Casper's, has become a cage she polishes daily. Beat: identity as performance wearing thin.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: A gale traps Elodie and Casper together in the society's flooded archive while salvaging festival records. Strangers still, they talk for hours by lantern light—about fear, fathers, and the books that saved them. Beat: connection without names, dangerously real.

chapters.title: Drafts Never Sent
chapters.summary: Alternating unsent letters. 'C' drafts a confession naming himself and burns it. 'E' drafts one admitting she knows what the Vanes intend and keeps writing anyway. Beat: both now lying knowingly, which is worse.

chapters.title: The Festival Committee
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The town votes to fight the development; Elodie is elected to lead, putting her directly across from Casper at the negotiating table. Their sparring has an edge neither can explain. Beat: enemies sharpening into fascination.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. His father offers him full partnership if he closes the lighthouse deal personally. Casper delays, sabotages the survey quietly, and tells 'E' he may soon do something unforgivable or redeeming—he isn't sure which. Beat: the choice taking shape.

chapters.title: Midnight at the Point
chapters.summary: Elodie climbs the lighthouse during a blackout and finds Casper already there, drawn by the same instinct. They almost kiss; she pulls back, saying she doesn't trust men who arrive with clipboards. Beat: desire checked by suspicion.

chapters.title: The Unmasking
chapters.summary: At the society's reveal evening, envelopes are opened. Elodie reads 'Casper Vane'; Casper reads 'Elodie Thackeray'—and then, from another member's slip, learns 'E' is also the famous novelist A. Merrick. Public humiliation compounds private betrayal. Beat: climax of deception.

chapters.title: Present Tense, Past Damage
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She tears up his letters, then rereads them instead, recognizing the man in the archive storm was true even if the correspondent wasn't. Casper, meanwhile, signs the demolition order under duress. Beat: grief and resolve entwined.

chapters.title: What Fathers Take
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Confronting his father, he discovers the original debt that ensnared the lighthouse was manufactured decades ago—a fraud his grandfather began. Casper copies the ledgers. Beat: inheritance reframed as evidence.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: At the festival's final night, Elodie reads aloud publicly as herself for the first time, claiming her name and her past heartbreak before the whole town. Casper listens from the back, holding the ledger copies. Beat: reclamation of identity.

chapters.title: Last Train Leaving
chapters.summary: Casper submits the forged-debt evidence to the council and resigns from Vane Development, forfeiting his inheritance and his father's approval in one signature. The festival ends; the last train departs without him. Beat: sacrifice made irreversible.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She expects emptiness after the crowds leave; instead Casper is on her doorstep, soaked, asking to stay—not for a night, but past every departure. She lets him in. Beat: vulnerability chosen over armor.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse Clause
chapters.summary: The council voids the fraudulent debt; the lighthouse passes to Elodie outright. Casper takes work restoring the harbour wall, rebuilding with his hands what his name had threatened. Beat: power renounced, purpose found.

chapters.title: A Novel in Present Tense
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Elodie begins a new book under her own name, co-dedicated to 'the man who missed the train.' Casper reads her draft pages each evening by the lamp they've relit together. Beat: love written forward, not backward.

chapters.title: Keepers
chapters.summary: One year later, festival night again. The light turns over the harbour; two keepers climb the stairs side by side. Elodie hands Casper a letter—their first, addressed openly, signed with real names. Beat: resolution—identity shared, inheritance rewritten, home kept together.
